meta.title: Who really said "Patience is a conquering virtue"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Chaucer's Franklin's Tale is the real source, but the four-word English phrasing is Nevill Coghill's 1951 translation of "Pacience is an heigh vertu."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Patience is a conquering virtue'?
meta.ogDescription: The thought is Chaucer's; the memorable wording is his 20th-century translator Nevill Coghill (Penguin Classics, 1951).

answer.label: Written by Geoffrey Chaucer
answer.authorDates: c. 1343–1400 · English poet, author of The Canterbury Tales
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from Chaucer’s “The Franklin’s Tale,” where the narrator praises patience in marriage. Chaucer’s own Middle English reads “Pacience is an heigh vertu, certeyn” — literally ‘a high virtue.’ The catchy “conquering virtue” is Nevill Coghill’s 1951 verse translation ↗, which reaches for the sense of the next line, “For it venquysseth…” (‘for it vanquishes’).

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
Patience is a conquering virtue.
The learned say that, if it not desert you,
It vanquishes what force can never reach;
Why answer back at every angry speech?
No, learn forbearance or, I’ll tell you what,
You will be taught it, whether you will or not.
trail: The line opens the Franklin’s praise of patience in a marriage — the passage is genuinely Chaucer’s Franklin’s Tale ↗.
Chaucer’s own words are Middle English: “Pacience is an heigh vertu, certeyn” ↗ — literally ‘a high virtue,’ not ‘a conquering virtue.’
The memorable English phrasing is Nevill Coghill’s 1951 rhyming translation ↗, first published in Penguin Classics ↗.
Quote sites paste the full stanza under “Geoffrey Chaucer” with no translator credit ↗.
source.excerptNote: Chaucer’s Middle English original: “Pacience is an heigh vertu, certeyn, / For it venquysseth, as thise clerkes seyn, / Thynges that rigour sholde nevere atteyne.”

source.rightsNote: The Middle English text of “The Franklin’s Tale” (c. 1400) has been in the public domain for centuries. But the exact English wording quoted here is Nevill Coghill’s verse translation, first published in Penguin Classics in 1951 and still under copyright — so this specific phrasing is not free to reuse.

author.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
author.heading: About Geoffrey Chaucer
author.metaLine: c. 1343–1400 · English poet & royal servant, the ‘Father of English literature’
author.bio: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was an English poet, courtier and civil servant best known for The Canterbury Tales, an unfinished set of stories told by pilgrims bound for Canterbury. Writing in the Middle English of his day, he helped make the vernacular a serious literary language. Because that verse is now hard to read, most modern readers meet him through translations — which is exactly how the wording of this quote came about.

misattribution.heading: The wording isn’t Chaucer’s
misattribution.intro: Crediting the line to Chaucer is essentially right — the thought and the source really are his. What gets lost is that the famous four-word English phrasing was written not by Chaucer but by his modern translator.

items.why: Chaucer wrote Middle English: “Pacience is an heigh vertu, certeyn” — ‘patience is a high virtue.’ The snappy “conquering virtue” is Nevill Coghill’s 1951 translation choice ↗, reaching forward to the next line’s “For it venquysseth” (‘for it vanquishes’).

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the source are genuinely Chaucer’s Franklin’s Tale ↗; the memorable phrasing belongs to his 20th-century translator, Nevill Coghill ↗.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: In “The Franklin’s Tale,” Chaucer’s narrator argues that a lasting marriage depends on patience: each partner must learn to endure the other’s faults, because “patience” wins what anger and force never can. It is one of the tale’s central moral threads.

The passage is a neat case study in how quotes travel. Chaucer’s hard-to-read Middle English is smoothed into a rhyming couplet by a translator, the translation becomes the ‘quote,’ and the translator’s name drops away — leaving readers to assume a medieval poet wrote a line no medieval reader ever saw.
context.pull: Chaucer supplied the thought; Coghill supplied the words.
